title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 35–36
description: Unit 35: media, broadcast genres, newspapers, magazines, advertising and news professions. Unit 36: problems at home and work, useful collocations, repair and apology language. Source-checked entries include original example sentences, British English IPA and Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt only.
sourceNotice: Content is organised from the textbook teaching pages, illustrations and exercises. All examples and usage notes are newly written; no complete exercises or copyrighted illustrations are reproduced. Exercise-only targets and pedagogical extensions are distinguished through contentOrigin.

audit.scope: Teaching pages, illustrations, common-mistakes box and learning tip, plus exercises 35.1–35.4 and 36.1–36.5, reviewed for core targets, collocations and contexts. All original item IDs preserved.

units.title: Unit 35 — The media
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 35. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: I listen to the radio while I cook.
items.note: Listen to the radio, but watch TV. The word radio usually takes the in this expression.

items.example: That radio programme starts at eight.
items.note: A programme broadcast on the radio. Programme is the usual British spelling for a broadcast; program is standard in computing.

items.example: We rarely watch TV during the week.
items.note: Usually say watch TV without the when talking about television as an activity.

items.example: This TV programme is suitable for children.
items.note: A particular show broadcast on television. Programme is standard British spelling in this context.

items.example: Which programme starts after the news?
items.note: A programme is one show; a channel broadcasts many programmes. British English generally uses programme for television.

items.example: The news is on at seven tonight.
items.note: News is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: the news is on, not the news are on.

items.example: My grandparents watch the news every evening.
items.note: Use watch for television and listen to for radio. You can also read the news online.

items.example: A new series is on TV tonight.
items.note: Be on TV means be broadcast on television. The subject is usually a show, programme or person.

items.example: We watch a soap together after dinner.
items.note: Short for soap opera in this context. Soap can also mean the substance used for washing.

items.pt: novela; série dramática de episódios frequentes
items.example: My uncle never misses his favourite soap opera.
items.note: A continuing drama about the daily lives and relationships of its characters, often broadcast frequently.

items.example: We watched a nature programme about sea birds.
items.note: A programme about the natural world, particularly animals and birds in the source.

items.example: They made a documentary about local hospitals.
items.note: A factual programme that explores an event, issue or subject. The source gives drugs and crime as examples of topics.

items.example: A writer appeared on a talk show yesterday.
items.note: A programme in which guests discuss topics or talk about themselves with a host or interviewer.

items.example: The interviewer asked her about her first job.
items.note: The person who asks questions in an interview. The person answering is the interviewee.

items.example: They discussed a difficult topic on the radio.
items.note: Discuss takes a direct object: discuss a topic, not discuss about a topic.

items.example: The children watched a cartoon before lunch.
items.note: Here a cartoon is an animated film or television programme. The same word can also refer to a drawing.

items.pt: programa de reality show; reality TV
items.example: Reality TV is popular with some of my friends.
items.note: Television featuring real people rather than characters played by actors; programmes can still be edited or produced.

items.example: My brother prefers sports programmes to dramas.
items.note: Sports acts as a modifier in sports programme and sports news.

items.example: We listen to international news on the radio.
items.note: Reports about events in different countries. This is a type of programme used in exercise 35.2; news is uncountable.

items.example: I read the sports news on my phone.
items.note: News about sport. Exercise 35.1 reinforces reading sports news on a mobile phone.

items.example: A newspaper is delivered to our office every day.
items.note: A newspaper publishes news and articles; a magazine usually collects articles on general or specialised topics.

items.example: I sometimes buy a morning newspaper at the station.
items.note: A newspaper published or sold in the morning, contrasted with an evening newspaper.

items.pt: jornal vespertino; jornal do fim da tarde
items.example: He reads an evening newspaper on his way home.
items.note: A newspaper published or sold later in the day; exercise 35.3 asks learners to recognise this meaning.

items.example: My sister bought a magazine at the airport.
items.note: A regular publication with articles and pictures. The source contrasts general magazines with specialised magazines.

items.example: The library has several women’s magazines.
items.note: Women is the irregular plural of woman; the apostrophe in women’s marks the plural possessive form.

items.example: He subscribes to a weekly news magazine.
items.note: A magazine mainly concerned with current events, rather than sport or another specialist topic.

items.example: She found a sports magazine in the waiting room.
items.note: A magazine focused on sport. Sports is normally plural in this compound.

items.example: My dad keeps some old computer magazines.
items.note: A magazine about computers or computing, listed among specialised magazines in the source.

items.example: He used to read a teenage magazine at school.
items.note: A magazine aimed at teenagers; the same category is reinforced in exercise 35.1.

items.example: I saw an advert for bicycles in the newspaper.
items.note: A common British English short form of advertisement. An advert tries to persuade people to buy something.

items.example: The newspaper has an advertisement for a new phone.
items.note: The full form of advert. The noun refers to paid promotional content, not to an impartial news report.

items.example: That TV advert is shown too often.
items.note: An advert shown on television. Exercise 35.4 asks learners whether they like watching adverts on TV.

items.pt: anúncio de; propaganda de um produto ou serviço
items.example: There was an advert for a bicycle in the paper.
items.note: Use an advert for something to name the product or service being advertised. This is a supporting collocation.

items.example: He sent me a newspaper article about transport.
items.note: An article is a piece of writing; a journalist can write articles for a newspaper or magazine.

items.example: I read an interview with a local musician.
items.note: An interview is a conversation in which one person asks another questions. The word can also be a verb.

items.example: There was an interview with the mayor on TV.
items.note: Use with to introduce the person being interviewed: an interview with a singer.

items.example: A reporter spoke to the people outside the hospital.
items.note: A reporter gathers and reports news where events happen. The source illustrates reporters near a film star’s house.

items.example: Her brother is a journalist for a local newspaper.
items.note: A journalist prepares news stories or articles. The source particularly describes someone writing for a newspaper.

items.example: The reporter found an important news story.
items.note: A journalistic report about an event; story in this sense does not mean a fictional tale.

items.example: She writes articles about education.
items.note: Write – wrote – written is irregular. Articles can appear in newspapers and magazines.

items.example: My cousin writes for a newspaper in Bristol.
items.note: Write for introduces the publication or organisation that publishes someone’s journalism.

items.pt: estrela de cinema; astro ou atriz de cinema
items.example: Several reporters waited for the film star.
items.note: A famous film actor. The source uses a film star to illustrate a situation involving reporters.

items.example: I read newspapers online before breakfast.
items.note: Online describes how the newspaper is accessed. Read is /riːd/ in the present but /red/ in the past.

items.example: My flatmates often watch TV online.
items.note: Watch TV online means view television content over the internet rather than only through traditional broadcasts.

items.example: My favourite TV programme is a science show.
items.note: Favourite is the British spelling of favorite. The phrase is used to talk about the programme you like most.

items.pt: O que está passando na TV?
items.example: What’s on TV after dinner?
items.note: What’s on TV? asks which programmes are being shown, not whether the television set is switched on.

items.example: That TV channel shows films all day.
items.note: A channel carries many programmes. Compare change the channel with watch a programme.

items.example: Could you change the channel, please?
items.note: A polite request is Is it OK if I change the channel? The object is the channel, not the programme.

items.pt: estar no ar; estar passando agora
items.example: The football match is on now.
items.note: The source illustrates the singular agreement of news in The news is on now. Be on describes a broadcast.

items.example: I downloaded a podcast for the journey.
items.note: The source’s Over to you activity suggests listening to programmes and downloading podcasts for extra practice.

learningObjectives: Identify common radio and television genres: soap operas, nature programmes, documentaries, talk shows, cartoons, reality TV and sports programmes.
Use the news with a singular verb and distinguish a programme from a TV channel.
Recognise morning and evening newspapers, general and specialist magazines, adverts and advertisements.
Explain the roles of reporters, journalists and interviewers, using interview with, write articles and write for a newspaper.
Ask what is on TV and politely request a change of channel.
Describe reading and viewing habits, including reading newspapers online and watching television online.

units.title: Unit 36 — Problems at home and work
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 36. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: The heating isn’t working today.
items.note: A device that is not working has stopped functioning. This is different from a person who is not working at a job.

items.example: The TV isn’t working, so we can listen to music.
items.note: A natural way to report a faulty television. Use is not working for a present problem with a device.

items.example: The phone isn’t working, so I cannot call the office.
items.note: Exercise 36.1 explicitly uses this sentence to describe a faulty phone. The same pattern applies to other devices.

items.example: Can you repair my old laptop?
items.note: Repair is normally transitive: repair a television or repair the machine. Compare mend.

items.example: My grandfather can mend bicycles.
items.note: Mend means repair something damaged, such as a bicycle or an item of clothing. The source uses it for a washing machine.

items.example: The handle on this door is broken.
items.note: Broken is the past participle of break: break – broke – broken. As an adjective it means damaged or not working.

items.example: We need someone to fix our broken washing machine.
items.note: Broken describes the state of the machine; mend or repair describes what needs to be done.

items.example: Our washing machine is in the kitchen.
items.note: A washing machine is a machine for washing clothes. The source introduces it as a household appliance that can break.

items.example: This plant needs more sunlight.
items.note: The source connects plants that are dying with the need to water them.

items.example: I moved the dying plants away from the radiator.
items.note: Dying is the -ing form of die, meaning coming to the end of life. Do not confuse die with dye.

items.example: Please water the plants before you leave.
items.note: Water can be a verb meaning give water to plants. It takes a direct object: water the plants.

items.example: I sometimes forget to water the flowers.
items.note: Forget to do something means fail to do it because you did not remember. Compare forget – forgot – forgotten.

items.example: His room is untidy after the party.
items.note: Untidy means not neat or organised; it is the opposite of tidy. It can describe a room, desk or bedroom.

items.example: Please tidy your desk before you leave.
items.note: As a verb, tidy means put things in order; as an adjective, it means neat. Clean focuses more on removing dirt.

items.pt: arrumar um cômodo; pôr um quarto em ordem
items.example: Could you tidy your room this afternoon?
items.note: Tidy takes a direct object. You can also say tidy up a room.

items.example: I often lose my keys when I am in a hurry.
items.note: Lose – lost – lost is irregular. Lose means no longer know where something is; do not confuse it with loose.

items.example: We found the lost keys under the sofa.
items.note: Lost is both the past form of lose and an adjective meaning missing.

items.example: I’m looking for my glasses.
items.note: Look for means search for someone or something; find means discover it. Look at means direct your eyes towards it.

items.example: Can you help me look for my keys?
items.note: Look for does not imply success. Help someone look for something is a natural pattern.

items.pt: cortar o dedo; ferir o dedo com um corte
items.example: Be careful not to cut your finger on the glass.
items.note: Cut – cut – cut is irregular but does not change form. Use a possessive determiner with a body part: cut your finger.

items.pt: cortar a mão; machucar a mão com um corte
items.example: He cut his hand while washing a glass.
items.note: The picture in exercise 36.1 shows an injured hand. Use a possessive determiner with a body part, as in cut your hand.

items.example: He had a small cut on his hand.
items.note: Cut can be a verb or a noun. The source uses a cut finger; this example illustrates the noun a cut.

items.example: There are some plasters in the first-aid box.
items.note: In this British English context, a plaster is a small adhesive dressing for a minor cut, also called a Band-Aid in American English.

items.example: She put on a plaster after washing the cut.
items.note: Put – put – put is irregular. Put on means apply a plaster to the injured area.

items.example: I had a row with my brother yesterday.
items.note: Here row means argument and is pronounced /raʊ/. Row meaning a line or a series is pronounced /rəʊ/.

items.pt: discutir com alguém; ter uma briga verbal
items.example: She had a row with her neighbour about the noise.
items.note: Use have a row with someone to identify the person involved in an argument.

items.example: He decided to apologise after the argument.
items.note: British spelling: apologise; American spelling: apologize. It means say that you are sorry.

items.example: I apologised to my colleague for being late.
items.note: Apologise to someone for something identifies the person and the reason. This preposition pattern extends the source.

items.example: When I realised my mistake, I said I was sorry.
items.note: The source explains apologise as saying I’m sorry. Quotation marks are not part of the spoken words.

items.word: have a bad day at work
items.pt: ter um dia ruim no trabalho
items.example: I had a bad day at work because the network failed.
items.note: A phrase that summarises several unpleasant events during the working day, as in the source story about Chloe.

items.example: She was late for work because she missed the bus.
items.note: Use late for work, school or an appointment to say someone arrives after the expected time.

items.example: The children were late for school on Monday.
items.note: Exercise 36.3 extends late for work to school. Both use late for.

items.example: We have too much work to finish before Friday.
items.note: Work is uncountable when it refers to tasks: too much work, not too many works.

items.example: I have too much to do this afternoon.
items.note: Have too much to do means have more tasks than you can comfortably finish. This is an extension of too much work to do.

items.example: A colleague helped me with the printer.
items.note: A colleague is someone you work with; they need not have exactly the same job.

items.example: My manager was in a bad mood all morning.
items.note: Use in a bad mood for someone who feels irritable or unhappy. The source describes a colleague this way.

items.example: A short break can sometimes help when you are in a bad mood.
items.note: Mood is a noun; use be in a bad mood rather than be with a bad mood.

items.example: A computer crash interrupted my work.
items.note: As a noun, crash means a sudden computer or software failure. The textbook presents the verb crashed.

items.pt: O computador travou; o sistema caiu.
items.example: My computer crashed while I was saving a file.
items.note: Crashed is the regular past tense of crash. A computer crash means the system suddenly stops working normally.

items.pt: travar; falhar de repente (sistema ou computador)
items.example: The application may crash if it runs out of memory.
items.note: In this computing context, crash means suddenly stop functioning; it does not mean a road collision.

items.example: The photocopier is next to the printer.
items.note: A photocopier makes copies of documents. The source says it was out of order.

items.example: The lift is out of order until tomorrow.
items.note: Out of order means a machine or facility is not working. It often appears on notices.

items.example: The coffee machine stopped working this morning.
items.note: A coffee machine makes coffee. In the source, the machine was not working.

items.example: I need to get up earlier to catch the first bus.
items.note: The example answer in exercise 36.4 suggests getting up earlier to avoid being late for work. Get up means leave bed.

items.example: I want to mend my bike this weekend.
items.note: The source’s learning tip includes Mend my bike as an example of a useful English to-do list item.

items.example: Please tidy your desk before you leave.
items.note: The source’s learning tip includes Tidy my desk as an English to-do list item.

items.example: I threw away a broken cup.
items.note: Exercise 36.1 shows broken crockery; exercise 36.2 suggests a cup as something that can be broken.

items.example: He does not like working in an untidy room.
items.note: The source describes a room as untidy and reinforces the idea with a picture in exercise 36.1.

learningObjectives: Describe common problems at home, such as broken appliances, dying plants, an untidy room, lost keys and minor injuries.
Use mend, repair, water, tidy, look for and put on a plaster appropriately when describing solutions.
Distinguish broken, not working, out of order and crashed in the contexts taught.
Describe an argument with have a row and explain an apology using apologise and I’m sorry.
Describe workplace difficulties such as being late, having too much work, a colleague in a bad mood and a computer crash.
Combine common adjectives and verbs with appropriate nouns and suggest solutions to everyday problems.
